refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: git-crypt enables transparent encryption and decryption of files in a git repository. Files which you choose to protect are encrypted when committed, and decrypted when checked out. git-crypt lets you freely share a repository containing a mix of public and private content. git-crypt gracefully degrades, so developers without the secret key can still clone and commit to a repository with encrypted files. This lets you store your secret material (such as keys or passwords) in the same repository as your code, without requiring you to lock down your entire repository.

refsect1.title: Commands
refsect1.para: git-crypt is logically divided into several sub-commands which perform distinct tasks. Each sub-command, and its arguments, are documented below. Note that arguments and options to sub-commands must be specified on the command line after the name of the sub-command.

listitem.para: Generate a key and prepare the current Git repository to use git-crypt.
The following options are understood:
Initialize the given key instead of the default key. git-crypt supports multiple keys per repository, allowing you to share different files with different sets of collaborators.

Generate a new key even though the repository already uses this key: it has GPG users for it in the .git-crypt directory, or files encrypted with it. Without this option, init refuses, because in a clone of an encrypted repository you almost certainly want git-crypt unlock instead: a new key cannot decrypt the existing files.
Display a list of files in the repository, with their status (encrypted or unencrypted).
The following options are understood:
Show only encrypted files.
Show only unencrypted files.

Encrypt files that should be encrypted but were committed to the repository or added to the index without encryption. (This can happen if a file is added before git-crypt is initialized or before the file is added to the gitattributes file.)

A file can only be encrypted while its key is unlocked. If the key is locked (for example because the file was staged while the repository was locked), the index entry is left unchanged, an error is printed, and the exit status is non-zero: run git-crypt unlock first.
Don't list untracked files. This is the default if Git's status.showUntrackedFiles option is set to no, which is useful in repositories with many untracked files (such as build output).

Instead of listing files, show whether each key used by the repository is locked or unlocked, one line per key (for example "default: unlocked" or "prod: locked"). A key is unlocked when its decrypted key is installed and its Git filter is configured. The exit status is 0 if every key is unlocked (or the repository uses no git-crypt keys) and 1 if any key is locked. The answer is the same from any worktree or subdirectory of the repository. This option cannot be combined with -e, -u, -f, or file names.
Don't write anything to standard output. The exit status is unchanged, so scripts can test it, e.g. git-crypt status -r -q || git-crypt unlock.

Add the users with the given GPG user IDs as collaborators. Specifically, git-crypt uses gpg1 to encrypt the shared symmetric key to the public keys of each GPG user ID, and stores the GPG-encrypted keys in the .git-crypt directory at the root of the repository.
GPG_USER_ID can be a key ID, a full fingerprint, an email address, or anything else that uniquely identifies a public key to GPG (see "HOW TO SPECIFY A USER ID" in the gpg1 man page).

To encrypt to one particular subkey (for example a new encryption subkey, while an older one is still valid), give the subkey's full fingerprint followed by an exclamation mark, optionally prefixed with 0x, e.g. 0x08E1C52060E273C858E45268928A04A1479EDD06!. The subkey must be able to encrypt and must not be expired or revoked. The collaborator's file is still named after their primary key's fingerprint.
A full fingerprint prefixed with 0x (with or without the trailing exclamation mark) identifies a key unambiguously, so it is treated as trusted, as with --trusted.
If a user has already been added to the key, they are skipped with a message, unless --force is given.
The following options are understood:
Grant access to the given key, rather than the default key.
Don't automatically commit the changes to the .git-crypt directory.
Assume that the GPG keys specified on the command line are trusted; i.e. they actually belong to the users that they claim to belong to.
Without this option, git-crypt uses the same trust model as GPG, which is based on the Web of Trust by default. Under this model, git-crypt will reject GPG keys that do not have trusted signatures.

If you don't want to use the Web of Trust, you can either change GPG's trust model by setting the trust-model option in ~/.gnupg/gpg.conf (see gpg1), or use the --trusted option to add-gpg-user on a case-by-case basis.
Re-encrypt the key to users who have already been added, replacing their existing file. Use this after a user changes encryption subkeys.

List the GPG collaborators who can unlock the repository: the fingerprints of the GPG keys that each key has been encrypted to by add-gpg-user, grouped by key name and key version. Where the fingerprint is in your GPG keyring, its user ID is shown. This reads the .git-crypt directory (or the directory set by git-crypt.repoStateDir), so it works whether or not the repository is unlocked. For example:
listitem.screen: Key 'default', version 0: 7A399B2DB06D039020CD1CE1D0F3702D61489532 John Smith <jsmith@example.com> 0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF01234567 (not in your GPG keyring)
listitem.para: The following options are understood:
List the collaborators of the given key only.

Decrypt the repository. If one or more key files are specified on the command line, git-crypt attempts to decrypt using those shared symmetric keys. If a KEY_FILE is -, the key is read from standard input instead of a file, which lets a key be supplied by a pipe without writing it to disk, e.g. echo "$KEY_BASE64" | base64 -d | git-crypt unlock -. If no key files are specified, git-crypt attempts to decrypt using a GPG-encrypted key stored in the repository's .git-crypt directory.
The decrypted keys are shared by all of the repository's worktrees, so unlocking (and locking) applies to every worktree at once. Every worktree must be clean.
The following options are understood:
After unlocking, list the files that were decrypted, grouped by key (and by worktree, if the repository has several), for example:

Remove the decrypted key from the repository, de-configure the git-crypt filters, and re-encrypt the encrypted files in every worktree. Every worktree must be clean, unless --force is given. Locking an already-locked key is an error, unless --if-unlocked is given.
The following options are understood:
Lock the given key, rather than the default key.
Lock all keys, rather than just the default key.
Lock even if a worktree has uncommitted changes. Uncommitted changes to encrypted files may be lost.

If the key is already locked (with --all: if no key is unlocked), do nothing and exit with status 0, without checking whether the worktrees are clean. Otherwise, lock as usual. This makes git-crypt lock --if-unlocked safe to run from cleanup scripts and CI trap handlers.
After locking, list the files that were re-encrypted, grouped by key (and by worktree, if the repository has several).

Rewrite the Git filter and textconv commands of every unlocked key, so that they run the program named by git-crypt.program if it is set, and the bare name git-crypt otherwise (see Configuration). Run it after setting or changing git-crypt.program, or when the filter commands name a git-crypt binary that no longer exists. It needs neither a key nor a clean working tree, prints an old -> new line on standard error for each key whose commands changed, and does nothing in a locked repository. It takes no options.
Export the repository's shared symmetric key to the given file. If FILENAME is -, the key is written to standard output instead.
The following options are understood:
Export the given key, rather than the default key.
Display help for the given COMMAND, or an overview of all commands if no command is specified.
Print the currently-installed version of git-crypt. The format of the output is always "git-crypt", followed by a space, followed by the dotted version number.

refsect1.title: Using git-crypt
refsect1.para: First, you prepare a repository to use git-crypt by running git-crypt init.
Then, you specify the files to encrypt by creating a gitattributes5 file. Each file which you want to encrypt should be assigned the "filter=git-crypt diff=git-crypt" attributes. For example:

Like a .gitignore file, .gitattributes files can match wildcards and should be checked into the repository. Make sure you don't accidentally encrypt the .gitattributes file itself (or other git files like .gitignore or .gitmodules). Make sure your .gitattributes rules are in place before you add sensitive files, or those files won't be encrypted!
To share the repository with others (or with yourself) using GPG, run:

GPG_USER_ID can be a key ID, a full fingerprint, an email address, or anything else that uniquely identifies a public key to GPG. Note: git-crypt add-gpg-user will add and commit a GPG-encrypted key file in the .git-crypt directory of the root of your repository.
Alternatively, you can export a symmetric secret key, which you must securely convey to collaborators (GPG is not required, and no files are added to your repository):
After cloning a repository with encrypted files, unlock with with GPG:
Or with a symmetric key:
That's all you need to do - after git-crypt is set up (either with git-crypt init or git-crypt unlock), you can use git normally - encryption and decryption happen transparently.

refsect1.title: The .gitattributes file
refsect1.para: The .gitattributes file is documented in gitattributes5. The file pattern format is the same as the one used by .gitignore, as documented in gitignore5, with the exception that specifying merely a directory (e.g. "/dir/") is not sufficient to encrypt all files beneath it.
Also note that the pattern "dir/*" does not match files under sub-directories of dir/. To encrypt an entire sub-tree dir/, place the following in dir/.gitattributes:
The second pattern is essential for ensuring that .gitattributes itself is not encrypted.

refsect1.title: Verifying encryption
refsect1.para: To check that files are stored encrypted, run git-crypt status. It lists every file, with "encrypted" or "not encrypted" according to .gitattributes:
refsect1.screen: $ git-crypt status not encrypted: .gitattributes not encrypted: README encrypted: secrets/api.txt
refsect1.para: For files that should be encrypted, status also checks the version stored in the index and in HEAD, and warns if it is plaintext:
refsect1.screen:
$ git-crypt status not encrypted: .gitattributes not encrypted: README encrypted: early.txt *** WARNING: staged/committed version is NOT ENCRYPTED! *** encrypted: secrets/api.txt
Warning: one or more files is marked for encryption via .gitattributes but was staged and/or committed before the .gitattributes file was in effect. Run 'git-crypt status' with the '-f' option to stage an encrypted version.
refsect1.para: This happens when a file was staged or committed before git-crypt was set up or before the file was covered by .gitattributes. git-crypt status -f stages an encrypted version (commit it afterwards). It can only do so while the key is unlocked; if the repository is locked it fails and asks you to run git-crypt unlock first.
refsect1.screen: $ git-crypt status -f early.txt: staged encrypted version Staged 1 encrypted file. Warning: if these files were previously committed, unencrypted versions still exist in the repository's history.
refsect1.para: The warning "diff=git-crypt attribute not set" means a file has filter=git-crypt but no diff=git-crypt in .gitattributes. The file is still encrypted, but git diff cannot show readable changes. git-crypt status exits with status 1 if it prints either warning.

To check without relying on git-crypt, read the stored blob directly. Encrypted blobs begin with the 10 bytes \0GITCRYPT\0 (a NUL byte, the string "GITCRYPT", and another NUL byte). Use HEAD:path for the committed version and :path for the staged version:
refsect1.screen: $ git cat-file -p HEAD:secrets/api.txt | head -c 10 | xxd 00000000: 0047 4954 4352 5950 5400 .GITCRYPT. $ git cat-file -p :secrets/api.txt | head -c 10 | od -c 0000000 \0 G I T C R Y P T \0
refsect1.para: Do not use git diff or git show to verify encryption. While the repository is unlocked, the diff=git-crypt attribute makes Git decrypt blobs (via textconv) for display, so they show plaintext even though the stored data is encrypted. Use --no-textconv to see what is stored:
refsect1.screen: $ git show --no-textconv HEAD -- secrets/api.txt ... diff --git a/secrets/api.txt b/secrets/api.txt index 5150825..9df0775 100644 Binary files a/secrets/api.txt and b/secrets/api.txt differ
refsect1.para: While the repository is locked, git diff, git diff --cached and git show print "Binary files ... differ" for these files whether or not they are encrypted (a plaintext file staged while locked looks the same), so they are not a check either.

git-crypt status examines the current index and HEAD only, not history. A file committed unencrypted earlier remains readable in older commits even after it is fixed; removing it requires rewriting history. A separate document on rewriting history is planned.

refsect1.title: Multiple Key Support
refsect1.para: In addition to the implicit default key, git-crypt supports alternative keys which can be used to encrypt specific files and can be shared with specific GPG users. This is useful if you want to grant different collaborators access to different sets of files.
To generate an alternative key named KEYNAME, pass the -k KEYNAME option to git-crypt init as follows:
To encrypt a file with an alternative key, use the git-crypt-KEYNAME filter in .gitattributes as follows:
To export an alternative key or share it with a GPG user, pass the -k KEYNAME option to git-crypt export-key or git-crypt add-gpg-user as follows:
refsect1.screen: git-crypt export-key -k KEYNAME /path/to/keyfile git-crypt add-gpg-user -k KEYNAME GPG_USER_ID
refsect1.para: To unlock a repository with an alternative key, use git-crypt unlock normally. git-crypt will automatically determine which key is being used.

refsect1.title: Git workflow notes
refsect1.para: Git stores the encrypted contents of protected files, and only git-crypt's filters turn them back into plaintext. Git features that look at stored file contents directly, or that choose a filter from the wrong .gitattributes, therefore misbehave in the ways described below. The examples were checked with Git 2.56; the exact wording of Git's messages differs between versions.

listitem.para: If an encrypted file changed on both sides, Git merges the encrypted blobs, which it treats as binary, so the merge conflicts without leaving conflict markers:
listitem.screen: warning: Cannot merge binary files: secret.txt (HEAD vs. other) CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in secret.txt
listitem.para: The working tree file just holds your side's plaintext. Locking does not help, because the blobs are encrypted either way. Stay unlocked and either pick one side:
listitem.screen: git checkout --theirs secret.txt git add secret.txt
listitem.para: or do a three-way merge of the decrypted versions (git cat-file --textconv decrypts each conflict stage) and edit any markers that remain before staging the result:
listitem.screen: gd=$(git rev-parse --git-dir) git cat-file --textconv :1:secret.txt > $gd/merge-base git cat-file --textconv :3:secret.txt > $gd/merge-theirs git cat-file --textconv :2:secret.txt > secret.txt git merge-file -L ours -L base -L theirs \ secret.txt $gd/merge-base $gd/merge-theirs rm $gd/merge-base $gd/merge-theirs git add secret.txt git commit
listitem.para: During a rebase, use git rebase --continue instead of git commit. During a rebase or cherry-pick, "ours" and "theirs" are swapped, as usual in Git. git-crypt does not currently provide a merge driver.
On an encrypted file, git add -p prints
because it builds hunks from the stored (encrypted) contents, which Git considers binary. This cannot be fixed within git-crypt. Stage the whole file instead:
Checking out a branch whose encrypted files were made with a different key (for example, history fetched from a repository that was initialized separately) fails:
listitem.screen: git-crypt: error: encrypted file has been tampered with! error: external filter '"git-crypt" smudge' failed 1 error: external filter '"git-crypt" smudge' failed fatal: secret.txt: smudge filter git-crypt failed
listitem.para: The checkout is aborted and leaves the file deleted from the working tree (git restore secret.txt brings it back). A branch where a file marked for encryption was committed as plaintext prints "git-crypt: warning: file not encrypted (run 'git-crypt status' for details)", and afterwards git status shows the file as modified and switching away fails with "Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout". In both cases, lock before switching and unlock afterwards with the key that belongs to the branch:
listitem.screen: git-crypt lock git checkout other-branch git-crypt unlock /path/to/key

listitem.para: Git picks the filter for a path from the .gitattributes of the commit or working tree you are currently on. Operations that read a single file from another branch therefore use the wrong key if the two branches encrypt that file with different keys. With secret using the default key on main and git-crypt-team on moved, git checkout moved -- secret and git diff main moved -- secret both fail with the "encrypted file has been tampered with!" error shown above.

Switching to the branch (git checkout moved) works, since the attributes switch with it. To read a file as it is on another branch without switching, tell Git to use that branch's attributes (needs Git 2.40 or later), and compare the two sides yourself:
listitem.screen: git --attr-source=moved cat-file --textconv moved:secret diff -u <(git --attr-source=main cat-file --textconv main:secret) \ <(git --attr-source=moved cat-file --textconv moved:secret)
listitem.para: git diff --no-textconv main moved -- secret also works, but only reports that the binary files differ.

varlistentry.term: git filter-branch and other history rewrites

listitem.para: After a rewrite that removes or changes the .gitattributes rule for an encrypted file, or if a file marked for encryption was committed as plaintext, the committed blob no longer matches what the filters produce from the working tree, so the tree looks dirty and the next rewrite refuses to run:
listitem.screen: Cannot rewrite branches: You have unstaged changes.
listitem.para: Lock before rewriting, so that git-crypt's filters are out of the way, and unlock afterwards:
listitem.screen: git-crypt lock git filter-branch ... git-crypt unlock /path/to/key
listitem.para: git-crypt lock itself refuses to run on a dirty tree, so if the tree is already dirty because of plaintext in history, do the rewrite in a fresh clone instead (a clone has no git-crypt filters configured until you unlock it).

core.autocrlf=true by itself does not damage encrypted files: git-crypt's output is detected as binary, and Git leaves it alone. Rules that force text handling of a path do damage them, because Git then converts line endings inside the encrypted data. Examples are "*.txt text" and "* text eol=crlf", with or without core.autocrlf=true. Signs of trouble are warnings like "in the working copy of 'secret.txt', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it" and, on checkout or git-crypt unlock, the "encrypted file has been tampered with!" error. Mark encrypted paths as not text:
eol=lf is not a substitute for -text. Make sure the -text rule comes after any broader rule that sets text or eol for the same path.
A path can have only one filter attribute, so combining the git-crypt and git-lfs filters on the same path is not supported. If two lines of .gitattributes both match a path, the last one wins:
listitem.screen:
*.bin filter=git-crypt diff=git-crypt *.bin filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
$ git check-attr filter -- a.bin a.bin: filter: lfs
listitem.para: Here the file is handled by git-lfs and is not encrypted. Use different paths for files handled by git-crypt and files handled by git-lfs.

varlistentry.term: GUI clients that cannot find git-crypt

listitem.para: The filter commands run git-crypt by its bare name, which is looked up on the PATH of whoever runs Git. A GUI that does not inherit your shell's PATH then fails:
listitem.screen: "git-crypt" smudge: git-crypt: command not found error: external filter '"git-crypt" smudge' failed 127 error: external filter '"git-crypt" smudge' failed fatal: secret.txt: smudge filter git-crypt failed
listitem.para: Point git-crypt at its absolute path with git-crypt.program (see Configuration) and rewrite the filters of each repository that is already unlocked:

refsect1.title: Configuration
refsect1.para: git-crypt reads the following options from the Git configuration (see git-config1):

listitem.para: When Git checks out a file that should be encrypted but whose blob is not (for example an old version committed before the file was added to .gitattributes), git-crypt passes it through unchanged and prints a one-line warning:
listitem.screen: git-crypt: warning: file not encrypted (run 'git-crypt status' for details)
listitem.para: Commands that walk history, such as git log -p or git blame, may print it many times. Set this boolean option to false to suppress the warning, e.g. git config git-crypt.warnUnencrypted false. Defaults to true. Use git-crypt status to check that the current files are properly encrypted.

Directory, relative to the top of the work tree, that holds the committed git-crypt state (the GPG-encrypted keys in keys/). Defaults to .git-crypt. This is local Git configuration and is not committed, so it must be set in every clone. It does not move the unlocked key, which always lives in the Git directory (see Files). Absolute paths are not supported: the value is appended to the path of the top of the work tree.
For example, to use a project that has its own .git-crypt directory and was added with git subtree add --prefix=sub REPOSITORY BRANCH:
listitem.screen: git config git-crypt.repoStateDir sub/.git-crypt git-crypt unlock

listitem.para: The program that the Git filter and textconv commands run. By default they run the bare name git-crypt, looked up on the PATH of whoever runs Git, even if you ran git-crypt by an absolute path, so the repository keeps working when git-crypt is upgraded or moved. Set this option to an absolute path to run a specific binary, for example for a Git GUI client that does not inherit your shell's PATH. The value must be an absolute path or a bare command name; an empty value or a relative path containing / is rejected. It is read with the usual git config lookup (system, global, then local).

The value is copied into the filter commands when they are written, by git-crypt init, git-crypt unlock and git-crypt refresh-filters, so after setting or changing it, run git-crypt refresh-filters in each unlocked repository:

A malicious directory on your PATH could run its own git-crypt and see your plaintext, but it could equally shadow git or gpg, so the bare name adds no new risk. An absolute path has the opposite trade-off: the repository breaks if that file is moved.
The unlocked symmetric key. NAME is default for the default key. Never committed. Shared by all linked worktrees. Created by git-crypt init and git-crypt unlock; removed by git-crypt lock.

Committed copy of the key encrypted to one collaborator's GPG key, named by the key's full fingerprint. Created by git-crypt add-gpg-user and listed by git-crypt ls-gpg-users. The leading .git-crypt directory can be changed with git-crypt.repoStateDir.
The raw symmetric key. Anyone who has it can decrypt the repository, so protect it like a password.
